title: Why Your Hotel's Information Goes Stale
summary: A hotel's answers live in four or five places at once and none of them has an owner, so they go out of date without anyone noticing. Why room descriptions go stale, where the answers actually live, and how to check your own property.
body_markdown:
Common questions


## FAQ


### Why does my hotel's room description say air conditioning when the room does not have it?


Because in many property management systems the room attributes are not structured data. Details like bed type, bathroom type and air conditioning often sit in a free-text comment box attached to the room category, typed in by a person.


At one German hotel group those boxes were maintained until 2022 in one part of the estate and until May 2026 in another, then stopped being updated after a booking engine was retired. A description can therefore promise a feature the category never had, or one it has since lost, with nothing on screen to indicate the text is out of date.


It matters most in summer: operators report that air conditioning inquiries surge with the first heat wave and that many guests will not book a room without one.


### Why do two people at my hotel give guests different answers to the same question?


Because the answer is not stored in one place, so each of them is reading a different source. Property data sits in free-text fields in the PMS. Internal procedure sits on SharePoint, in an internal wiki, or in a PDF somebody emailed.


A meaningful share of it sits only in the memory of whoever has worked there longest, and that person is not on every shift. None of these sources has a single owner, and none of them carries a date that tells a colleague it has gone stale. What a guest hears therefore depends on which source the person who answered reached first.


If two colleagues on different shifts answer the same question differently, that is not a training gap. It is proof the answer was never written down in the first place.


### Why does hotel information go out of date so quickly?


Because operations move faster than documentation and nothing forces the two back together. Most mistakes in a hotel announce themselves: an unclean room gets a complaint, a wrong invoice gets a phone call. A room description that is three years out of date announces nothing, so no routine catches it. Operational facts drift fastest of all.


Reception hours change from a given Monday, and every document saying otherwise still reads as perfectly plausible. On top of that, each renovation, rate change, retired system, merged property and departing colleague adds a fact that was true once, and very little ever removes one, so the stock of stale information grows on its own.


### Where do hotels actually store the answers their staff need?


Usually across four places at once, with no single owner. Property data sits in free-text fields in the PMS. Internal knowledge sits on SharePoint or an internal wiki, including at one group of more than 100 hotels across two countries whose own assessment is that not everybody has access and it is always out of date.


Procedure sits in PDFs sent by email, which one food and beverage lead described as useless to kitchen staff mid-shift. And a meaningful share sits only in individual memory: at one property, post-checkout luggage storage is free but only on the departure day, because the luggage room is small, a rule that is correct and was never written down.


Parking is a common case where the information is not in the PMS at all.


### What does a wrong answer cost a hotel?


There is no honest single figure for this, and any vendor quoting one is guessing. The reason is structural: a hotel cannot connect a completed booking back to the answer given on a call, and it certainly cannot connect a booking that never happened to a wrong answer nobody recorded. What can be described is the shape of the cost.


A guest given a confidently wrong answer books, arrives, finds the room does not match, and writes a review that reads as a complaint about honesty rather than about data, which the hotel then attributes to the room. A guest given no answer at all simply calls the next hotel, and that one leaves no trace anywhere.


Neither outcome arrives labelled as an information problem, which is why most properties conclude they do not have one.


### How can I tell whether my own hotel has this problem?


Test it directly, because almost no property has a report that would show it. Call your own hotel and ask something specific that is not published on your website, then count how many places the person has to look. Read your room category descriptions in the PMS as a guest would and find out when they were last edited and who owns them.


Ask two colleagues on different shifts the same question separately, and treat any difference as proof the answer is not written down. Check the category descriptions at your most recently renovated or most recently merged property against what is physically in those rooms now. Finally, ask for a list of the questions your team could not answer last week.


Most hotels cannot produce one, and that absence is itself the answer.
